history.q: At the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE, Athenians defeated an invading army from which empire?
history.fact: The legend of a messenger running from Marathon to Athens inspired the marathon race, first run at the 1896 Athens Olympics.

history.q: Which Macedonian king built an empire stretching from Greece to India?
history.fact: Tutored as a teenager by Aristotle, Alexander founded many cities bearing his name, most famously Alexandria in Egypt.

history.q: Which Spartan king led the Greek stand at Thermopylae in 480 BCE?
history.fact: The famous 300 Spartans fought alongside thousands of other Greeks, including about 700 Thespians who also stayed to the end.

history.q: During the Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE), which city-state led the alliance that fought Athens?
history.fact: The war's great chronicler, Thucydides, was himself an Athenian general who was exiled after a military failure.

history.q: In which year did the Greek War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire begin?
history.fact: Greece celebrates Independence Day on 25 March, the same day as the Orthodox Feast of the Annunciation.

history.q: The Bronze Age Minoan civilisation was centred on which island?
history.fact: The palace of Knossos, excavated by Arthur Evans from 1900, is linked in legend to the Minotaur's labyrinth.

history.q: In which year did Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire, fall to the Ottomans?
history.fact: The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, died defending the city's walls on 29 May 1453.

history.q: Which Athenian statesman masterminded the Greek naval victory at Salamis in 480 BCE?
history.fact: Themistocles had earlier persuaded Athens to spend a windfall from its Laurion silver mines on building a fleet of warships.

history.q: Which 1827 naval battle, won by British, French and Russian fleets, proved decisive for Greek independence?
history.fact: Fought off modern Pylos, Navarino was the last major naval battle fought entirely with wooden sailing ships.

history.q: Which town served as Greece's capital before the seat of government moved to Athens in 1834?
history.fact: Ioannis Kapodistrias, independent Greece's first head of state, was assassinated outside a church in Nafplio in 1831.

history.q: Which Athenian philosopher was sentenced to death in 399 BCE and made to drink hemlock?
history.fact: Socrates wrote nothing himself; we know his ideas mainly through the dialogues of his student Plato.

history.q: Which Persian king led the great invasion of Greece in 480 BCE?
history.fact: For the invasion, Xerxes had a bridge of boats built across the Hellespont and a canal dug through the Athos peninsula.

history.q: Which sanctuary was home to the most famous oracle of ancient Greece, the Oracle of Apollo?
history.fact: Greeks believed Delphi was the centre of the world, marked by a sacred stone called the omphalos, or 'navel'.

history.q: Which Greek writer is often called the 'Father of History'?
history.fact: Herodotus came from Halicarnassus, modern Bodrum in Turkey, and his Histories chronicle the wars between the Greeks and Persians.

history.q: The ancient Olympic Games were held in honour of which god?
history.fact: Olympia's gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus, made by the sculptor Phidias, was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

history.q: Which Macedonian king, father of Alexander the Great, was assassinated in 336 BCE?
history.fact: Philip was stabbed by his bodyguard Pausanias during his daughter's wedding celebrations at Aegae, the old Macedonian royal capital.

history.q: Which country invaded Greece on 28 October 1940, after Greece rejected its ultimatum?
history.fact: Greeks celebrate 'Ochi Day' ('No Day') every 28 October, recalling Prime Minister Metaxas's refusal of Mussolini's ultimatum.

history.q: Which Bronze Age civilisation, named after a citadel with a famous Lion Gate, dominated mainland Greece?
history.fact: Heinrich Schliemann found the gold 'Mask of Agamemnon' at Mycenae in 1876, though it predates the legendary king by centuries.

history.q: Under the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne, Greece agreed a compulsory population exchange with which country?
history.fact: About 1.2 million Orthodox Christians left Anatolia for Greece, and around 400,000 Muslims moved from Greece to Turkey.

history.q: In which year did German occupation forces withdraw from Athens during the Second World War?
history.fact: Athens was liberated on 12 October 1944, after three and a half years of occupation marked by a terrible famine.

history.q: Which Theban general broke Sparta's military power at the Battle of Leuctra in 371 BCE?
history.fact: Epaminondas went on to free the Messenians, long held as helots by Sparta, and founded the city of Messene for them.

history.q: In which year did the Greek Civil War end?
history.fact: Fought between the government army and Communist-led forces, it was one of the first conflicts of the Cold War.

history.q: Which King of Greece was assassinated in Thessaloniki in 1913?
history.fact: Born a Danish prince, George I had reigned for almost 50 years; he was shot while out walking in the newly won city.

history.q: Which island group did Britain hand over to Greece in 1864?
history.fact: The islands had been a British protectorate since 1815; Britain ceded them partly to support Greece's new king, George I.

history.q: In 146 BCE, the same year Carthage was razed, Rome destroyed which Greek city?
history.fact: Julius Caesar refounded Corinth as a Roman colony in 44 BCE, and it later became the capital of the province of Achaea.

technology.q: Which Greek mathematician of Syracuse is said to have shouted 'Eureka!' in his bath?
technology.fact: Archimedes also designed war machines to defend Syracuse against a Roman siege, which ended with his death in 212 BCE.

technology.q: Which ancient Greek physician is known as the 'father of medicine'?
technology.fact: Hippocrates came from the island of Kos and taught that diseases have natural causes rather than being punishments from the gods.

technology.q: Which Greek thinker gives his name to the theorem a² + b² = c²?
technology.fact: Pythagoras was born on the island of Samos, where the harbour town of Pythagoreio now bears his name.

technology.q: Which Greek mathematician wrote the 'Elements', the classic textbook of geometry?
technology.fact: Euclid worked in Alexandria around 300 BCE; his Elements served as the standard geometry textbook for over 2,000 years.

technology.q: The Antikythera mechanism, recovered from an ancient shipwreck in 1901, was used for what?
choices: Measuring the depth of the sea
technology.fact: Often called the world's first analogue computer, its corroded bronze gears are displayed at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

technology.q: Which Greek scholar estimated the Earth's circumference using shadows cast in two Egyptian cities?
technology.fact: Eratosthenes, chief librarian at Alexandria, is also credited with coining the word 'geography'.

technology.q: Hero of Alexandria described the aeolipile, a spinning sphere driven by what?
technology.fact: Hero also described a coin-operated holy-water dispenser, often called the world's first vending machine.

technology.q: Which ancient Greek astronomer is credited with the earliest known model placing the Sun at the centre of the cosmos?
technology.fact: Aristarchus also tried to measure the sizes and distances of the Sun and Moon, concluding the Sun was much larger than the Earth.

technology.q: Opened in 1893, the Corinth Canal links the Gulf of Corinth with which other gulf?
technology.fact: About 6.4 km long and only about 25 m wide at water level, the canal realised a project first attempted by Emperor Nero in 67 CE.

technology.q: Greek-born physician Georgios Papanikolaou pioneered a screening test for which disease?
technology.fact: Born in Kymi on the island of Euboea, Papanikolaou did his research in New York; his 'Pap test' has saved countless lives.

technology.q: Which philosopher, a student of Plato, wrote pioneering works on biology, logic and physics?
technology.fact: Aristotle founded the Lyceum in Athens; his followers were called Peripatetics, perhaps from his habit of walking while teaching.

technology.q: Which Greek letter stands for the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter?
technology.fact: Archimedes showed that pi lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7, though the symbol π itself was only popularised by Euler in the 1700s.

technology.q: Democritus taught that all matter is made of tiny, indivisible particles. What did he call them?
technology.fact: 'Atom' comes from the Greek 'atomos', meaning 'uncuttable'; Democritus came from Abdera in Thrace.

technology.q: Which device for raising water, a helix turning inside a tube, is traditionally credited to Archimedes?
technology.fact: Archimedes' screws are still used today, from sewage works to fish-friendly hydropower turbines.

technology.q: Which giant bronze statue of the sun god Helios, one of the Seven Wonders, stood on a Greek island harbour?
technology.fact: About 33 m tall, the Colossus stood for only around half a century before an earthquake toppled it, around 226 BCE.

technology.q: Which Alexandrian scholar's 'Almagest' set out the Earth-centred model of the cosmos that dominated astronomy for centuries?
technology.fact: Written around 150 CE, the Almagest remained the standard astronomy text in Europe and the Islamic world for over 1,400 years.

technology.q: Which Greek physician from Pergamon treated gladiators before becoming doctor to Emperor Marcus Aurelius?
technology.fact: Galen's writings, partly based on dissecting animals, dominated European medicine until Andreas Vesalius challenged them in the 1500s.

technology.q: Which philosopher of Miletus is said to have predicted a solar eclipse in 585 BCE?
technology.fact: Often called the first Greek philosopher, Thales proposed that everything is ultimately made of water.

technology.q: Which Alexandrian mathematician is often called the 'father of algebra' for his work 'Arithmetica'?
technology.fact: Pierre de Fermat scribbled his famous 'Last Theorem' in the margin of his copy of Diophantus' Arithmetica, around 1637.

technology.q: Which Alexandrian scholar, killed in 415 CE, is the earliest female mathematician whose life is reasonably well recorded?
technology.fact: Hypatia's father Theon produced an edition of Euclid's Elements; she taught philosophy and astronomy in Alexandria.

technology.q: Which Greek astronomer discovered the precession of the equinoxes and compiled an early star catalogue?
technology.fact: Hipparchus is often called the father of trigonometry, and the European Space Agency's star-mapping satellite Hipparcos was named after him.

technology.q: The Tunnel of Eupalinos, a 6th-century BCE aqueduct dug from both ends at once, is on which island?
technology.fact: The two digging teams met near the middle of the 1,036 m tunnel with only a small error, an astonishing feat of ancient surveying.

technology.q: The Rio-Antirrio Bridge, opened in 2004, spans which body of water?
technology.fact: At about 2.9 km, it is one of the world's longest multi-span cable-stayed bridges, designed to survive earthquakes and shifting tectonic plates.

technology.q: Which engineer of 3rd-century BCE Alexandria invented the hydraulis, a water-powered organ?
technology.fact: Often called the father of pneumatics, Ctesibius also built greatly improved water clocks.

technology.q: Which geometer wrote 'Conics', giving us the names ellipse, parabola and hyperbola?
technology.fact: The three names come from Greek words meaning roughly 'falling short', 'comparison' and 'excess'.

art.q: Who is traditionally credited as the author of the 'Iliad' and the 'Odyssey'?
art.fact: The Iliad is set during the Trojan War, while the Odyssey follows Odysseus' ten-year voyage home to Ithaca.

art.q: To which goddess was the Parthenon in Athens dedicated?
art.fact: Built in 447-432 BCE, the Parthenon was badly damaged in 1687 when a Venetian shell ignited Ottoman gunpowder stored inside.

art.q: The Venus de Milo statue, now in the Louvre, was found on which Greek island?
art.fact: Found by a farmer in 1820, the statue is thought to depict Aphrodite; her missing arms have never been found.

art.q: Which Greek-American soprano was nicknamed 'La Divina'?
art.fact: Born in New York to Greek parents, Callas spent her teenage years in Athens, where she trained at the conservatory.

art.q: Which Athenian playwright wrote the tragedy 'Oedipus Rex'?
art.fact: Sophocles is said to have written over 120 plays, but only seven complete tragedies survive.

art.q: The painter El Greco, famous for his work in Toledo, Spain, was born on which island?
art.fact: His real name was Domenikos Theotokopoulos; 'El Greco' simply means 'the Greek' in Spanish.

art.q: Which order of classical columns, the plainest of the three Greek orders, was used for the Parthenon's outer colonnade?
art.fact: The Parthenon's columns swell slightly in the middle, a technique called entasis that makes them look perfectly straight from afar.

art.q: Which ancient theatre in the Peloponnese is famed for acoustics so good that a whisper on stage carries to the back rows?
art.fact: Built in the 4th century BCE and seating around 14,000, the theatre still hosts plays every summer during the Epidaurus Festival.

art.q: Which Cretan author wrote the novel 'Zorba the Greek'?
art.fact: Kazantzakis' grave in Heraklion bears the epitaph: 'I hope for nothing. I fear nothing. I am free.'

art.q: Who became the first Greek to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1963?
art.fact: Seferis was also a career diplomat who served as Greek ambassador in London; Odysseas Elytis became Greece's second literature laureate in 1979.

art.q: Which Greek composer won an Oscar for his score for 'Chariots of Fire'?
art.fact: Vangelis, born Evangelos Papathanassiou, also composed the electronic score for Ridley Scott's 'Blade Runner' (1982).

art.q: Which ancient Athenian playwright wrote the comedies 'The Frogs' and 'Lysistrata'?
art.fact: In 'The Clouds', Aristophanes mocked Socrates, who is said to have stood up in the theatre so the audience could compare him with his mask.

art.q: Which Hellenistic statue of a winged goddess, found on Samothrace in 1863, towers over a staircase in the Louvre?
art.fact: The statue shows Nike, goddess of victory, alighting on a ship's prow; her name was later borrowed by the sportswear brand.

art.q: Which ancient Greek storyteller is credited with fables such as 'The Tortoise and the Hare'?
art.fact: According to Herodotus, Aesop was an enslaved man on the island of Samos; his fables were passed down orally for centuries.

art.q: Myron's famous ancient sculpture 'Discobolus' shows an athlete doing what?
art.fact: Myron's original 5th-century BCE bronze is lost; we know it today through Roman marble copies.

art.q: Which composer wrote the music for the 1964 film 'Zorba the Greek'?
art.fact: The film's famous sirtaki dance was choreographed for the movie rather than being a traditional folk dance, yet it became a symbol of Greece.

art.q: Which Athenian tragedian wrote 'Medea'?
art.fact: Euripides won relatively few prizes in his lifetime, yet more of his plays survive than those of Aeschylus and Sophocles combined.

art.q: Which sculptor oversaw the Parthenon's decoration and made its giant gold-and-ivory statue of Athena?
art.fact: The Athena Parthenos stood about 12 m tall; a full-size modern replica stands in a Parthenon replica in Nashville, Tennessee.

art.q: The Erechtheion on the Acropolis has a porch held up by statues of young women. What are these figures called?
art.fact: One of the six original Caryatids was taken by Lord Elgin and is in the British Museum; the other five are in Athens' Acropolis Museum.

art.q: Which Greek director made the films 'The Lobster' and 'Poor Things'?
art.fact: Lanthimos first won international attention with 'Dogtooth' (2009), which won a prize at Cannes and was nominated for an Oscar.

art.q: Which Alexandria-based poet wrote 'Ithaka' and 'Waiting for the Barbarians'?
art.fact: Cavafy spent most of his life in Alexandria, Egypt, working as a civil servant, and shared his poems mainly in privately printed sheets.

art.q: Which Greek director's 'Eternity and a Day' won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 1998?
art.fact: Angelopoulos, known for long, slow takes, died in 2012 after being struck by a motorcycle while filming near Piraeus.

art.q: Which Athenian dramatist wrote the 'Oresteia' trilogy?
art.fact: Aeschylus fought at Marathon, and his epitaph is said to have mentioned only his soldiering, not his plays.

art.q: Which bouzouki-based urban music, linked to refugees from Asia Minor, was added to UNESCO's cultural heritage list in 2017?
art.fact: Rebetiko flourished after 1922 in port cities like Piraeus, and was long frowned upon for songs about hashish dens and prison.

art.q: Which pioneer of 'metaphysical painting' was born in Volos, Greece, to Italian parents?
art.fact: De Chirico's eerie, empty piazzas and long shadows had a deep influence on the Surrealists.

politics.q: Democracy, meaning 'rule by the people', first developed in which ancient city-state?
politics.fact: Athenian citizens voted directly on laws in the Assembly, which met on the Pnyx hill facing the Acropolis.

politics.q: Which Athenian statesman led the city in its 5th-century BCE 'Golden Age' and championed building the Parthenon?
politics.fact: Pericles' famous Funeral Oration was recorded by the historian Thucydides; Pericles died during the plague of Athens in 429 BCE.

politics.q: In ancient Athens, what was the practice of voting to exile a citizen for ten years called?
politics.fact: Voters scratched names on pottery shards called ostraka; thousands of these have been excavated in Athens.

politics.q: Under its 1975 constitution, what is Greece's form of government?
politics.fact: Greece's president is elected by Parliament and is largely ceremonial; executive power lies with the Prime Minister and cabinet.

politics.q: Whose reforms of 508/507 BCE are traditionally seen as founding Athenian democracy?
politics.fact: Cleisthenes reorganised Athenian citizens into ten new tribes, breaking the power of old aristocratic clans.

politics.q: A military junta known as 'the Colonels' ruled Greece from 1967 until which year?
politics.fact: Greeks commemorate the November 1973 Athens Polytechnic uprising against the junta every year on 17 November.

politics.q: How many members sit in Greece's single-chamber Hellenic Parliament?
politics.fact: Parliament meets in the Old Royal Palace on Syntagma Square, originally built for King Otto.

politics.q: In which year did Greece join the European Economic Community?
politics.fact: Greece became the EEC's tenth member on 1 January 1981, five years before Spain and Portugal joined.

politics.q: Who was the last King of Greece, before the monarchy was abolished by referendum in 1974?
politics.fact: Before becoming king, Constantine won an Olympic gold medal in sailing at the 1960 Rome Games.

politics.q: Otto, the first king of modern Greece, was a prince from which German kingdom?
politics.fact: Otto arrived in Greece in 1833 aged just 17; he was deposed in 1862 and returned to Bavaria.

politics.q: Which Athenian lawgiver's code was so harsh that it gave English the word for 'excessively severe'?
politics.fact: Draco's laws of around 621 BCE were Athens' first written code; a later orator quipped they were written in blood, not ink.

politics.q: Which philosopher wrote 'The Republic', describing an ideal state ruled by philosopher-kings?
politics.fact: Plato founded the Academy in Athens around 387 BCE, the school that gave us the word 'academic'.

politics.q: Which currency did Greece replace with the euro?
politics.fact: The drachma's name goes back about 2,500 years to ancient Greek coins; euro notes and coins replaced it in 2002.

politics.q: What was the ancient Greek word for a self-governing city-state?
politics.fact: The English word 'politics' comes from polis, through the Greek 'politika', meaning the affairs of the city.

politics.q: Which Greek-derived word means 'rule by a few'?
politics.fact: In 411 BCE an oligarchic regime known as the Four Hundred briefly overthrew Athenian democracy.

politics.q: How many kings ruled ancient Sparta at the same time?
politics.fact: Sparta's two kings came from two royal houses, the Agiads and Eurypontids, and were overseen by five elected ephors.

politics.q: What are the ceremonial guards at Athens' Tomb of the Unknown Soldier called?
politics.fact: Each guard's pleated kilt, the fustanella, is said to have 400 pleats, one for each year of Ottoman rule.

politics.q: Which Cretan-born statesman served as Greek Prime Minister several times between 1910 and 1933 and gives his name to Athens' airport?
politics.fact: Venizelos led Greece through the Balkan Wars of 1912-13, which greatly enlarged the country's territory.

politics.q: Which Athenian lawgiver abolished debt slavery around 594 BCE?
politics.fact: Solon, also a poet, is counted among the Seven Sages of Greece; after his reforms he reportedly left Athens for ten years.

politics.q: Who returned from exile in 1974 to lead Greece's transition back to democracy after the junta fell?
politics.fact: Karamanlis founded the New Democracy party in 1974 and later served two terms as President of Greece.

politics.q: Which party did Andreas Papandreou found in 1974?
politics.fact: PASOK won the 1981 election, forming Greece's first socialist government; Andreas's father and son also became Prime Ministers.

politics.q: Ioannis Metaxas established his authoritarian regime on 4 August of which year?
politics.fact: Known as the '4th of August Regime', it lasted beyond Metaxas himself, who died in January 1941.

politics.q: In ancient Athens, which council of 500 citizens chosen by lot prepared business for the Assembly?
politics.fact: Its members served for one year, 50 from each of Athens' ten tribes, and no one could serve more than twice in a lifetime.

politics.q: Modern Greece's Supreme Civil and Criminal Court takes its name from which ancient Athenian council?
politics.fact: The ancient council met on a rocky hill below the Acropolis, where in myth the god Ares himself was put on trial.

politics.q: Which 19th-century Prime Minister, a champion of railways and the Corinth Canal, told Parliament in 1893 that Greece was bankrupt?
politics.fact: Trikoupis' long rivalry with Theodoros Deligiannis dominated Greek politics for two decades.

current-affairs.q: Which party won Greece's June 2023 parliamentary election outright?
current-affairs.fact: Kyriakos Mitsotakis, whose father Konstantinos was Prime Minister in 1990-93, began a second term as Prime Minister after the vote.

current-affairs.q: Greek basketball star Giannis Antetokounmpo won the 2021 NBA championship with which team?
current-affairs.fact: Born in Athens to Nigerian parents, Giannis scored 50 points in the title-clinching game and was named Finals MVP.

current-affairs.q: In April 2024, the Olympic flame was lit at Ancient Olympia for which Summer Games?
current-affairs.fact: The flame sailed from Greece to Marseille aboard the Belem, a three-masted ship built in the 19th century.

current-affairs.q: Which Greek city opened its long-awaited metro system in November 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Construction was slowed for years by spectacular Byzantine and Roman finds, some of which are now displayed inside the stations.

current-affairs.q: Who became Greece's first female President in March 2020?
current-affairs.fact: Sakellaropoulou, a judge, had previously been the first woman to lead Greece's Council of State, its supreme administrative court.

current-affairs.q: Which former Prime Minister stepped down as leader of SYRIZA after the 2023 elections?
current-affairs.fact: Tsipras became Prime Minister in January 2015 aged 40 and steered Greece through that summer's dramatic bailout referendum.

current-affairs.q: In 2024, which club became the first Greek side to win a major UEFA club trophy, the Europa Conference League?
current-affairs.fact: Olympiacos beat Fiorentina 1-0 in extra time, and the final happened to be played in Athens.

current-affairs.q: In February 2024, Greece became the first Orthodox Christian-majority country to legalise what?
current-affairs.fact: The same law also gave same-sex married couples the right to adopt children.

current-affairs.q: Who was elected President of Greece by Parliament in February 2025?
current-affairs.fact: Tasoulas had served as Speaker of the Hellenic Parliament before taking up the presidency in March 2025.

current-affairs.q: Miltiadis Tentoglou won Olympic gold at both Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 in which event?
current-affairs.fact: In Tokyo he tied Cuba's Juan Miguel Echevarría at 8.41 m with his final jump and took gold thanks to a better second-best leap.

current-affairs.q: In 2021, which player became the first Greek man to reach a Grand Slam singles final, at the French Open?
current-affairs.fact: Tsitsipas led Novak Djokovic by two sets to love in the final before losing in five sets.

current-affairs.q: In July 2023, wildfires forced around 19,000 people to evacuate on which Greek holiday island?
current-affairs.fact: Many of those moved to safety were tourists, in what officials described as Greece's largest-ever wildfire evacuation.

current-affairs.q: In February 2025, thousands of residents and workers left which famous Cycladic island amid an intense earthquake swarm?
current-affairs.fact: Thousands of tremors were recorded in the sea between Santorini and Amorgos, and schools closed on several islands as a precaution.

current-affairs.q: Which Athens basketball club won the EuroLeague in 2024?
current-affairs.fact: It was Panathinaikos' seventh EuroLeague crown, won against Real Madrid in the final in Berlin.

current-affairs.q: Under a deal with Greece that took effect in 2019, Greece's northern neighbour changed its name to what?
current-affairs.fact: The Prespa Agreement, named after the lake where it was signed in 2018, ended a naming dispute dating back to 1991.

current-affairs.q: Greece's deadliest rail accident, a head-on train collision in February 2023, happened near which valley?
current-affairs.fact: The crash killed 57 people and sparked mass protests across Greece over rail safety.

current-affairs.q: In September 2023, Storm Daniel caused catastrophic flooding across which Greek farming region?
current-affairs.fact: Storm Daniel then crossed the Mediterranean and devastated the Libyan city of Derna, where two dams collapsed.

current-affairs.q: In August 2021, wildfires devastated the north of which large island, Greece's second largest?
current-affairs.fact: Ferries evacuated hundreds of residents and tourists from Evia's beaches as the flames reached the shore.

current-affairs.q: In October 2024, Greece's footballers won at Wembley for the first time, beating which country?
current-affairs.fact: Vangelis Pavlidis scored both goals in a 2-1 win, days after the death of Greek international defender George Baldock.

current-affairs.q: In 2021, Greece took delivery of its first Rafale fighter jets from which country?
current-affairs.fact: Greece became the Rafale's first European export customer, eventually ordering 24 of the jets.

current-affairs.q: In August 2023, the largest wildfire ever recorded in the EU burned in which Greek region near the Turkish border?
current-affairs.fact: The fire burned over 80,000 hectares, including much of the Dadia Forest, an important refuge for vultures.

current-affairs.q: In March 2023, which state returned three fragments of the Parthenon sculptures to Greece?
current-affairs.fact: The fragments, the heads of a horse, a boy and a bearded man, went on display in Athens' Acropolis Museum.

current-affairs.q: Who was elected leader of SYRIZA in September 2023, succeeding Alexis Tsipras?
current-affairs.fact: A former Goldman Sachs trader who had lived in the United States, Kasselakis was little known in Greek politics before his election.

current-affairs.q: Which Greek tennis player reached the semi-finals of both the French Open and the US Open in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Sakkari's mother, Angeliki Kanellopoulou, was also a professional tennis player who ranked in the world's top 50 in the 1980s.

current-affairs.q: In April 2022, Greece repaid its remaining loans from which lender, about two years early?
current-affairs.fact: The IMF had been part of the 'troika' that oversaw Greece's bailouts from 2010, alongside the European Commission and the ECB.

society.q: In 2024, a Greek law came into force allowing some businesses to put staff on a working week of how many days?
society.fact: Law 5053/2023, in force from 1 July 2024, lets businesses operating around the clock schedule a sixth day paid at a 40% overtime premium; unions held strikes against it.

society.q: In 2023, Greece's sovereign credit rating regained which status for the first time since the 2010 debt crisis?
society.fact: DBRS, S&P and Fitch all upgraded Greece in late 2023, roughly 13 years after rating agencies first cut it to 'junk'.

society.q: International tourist arrivals in Greece reached a record of roughly how many in 2024?
society.fact: Bank of Greece data put arrivals at 40.7 million, almost four times the population of about 10.5 million, fuelling debate about overtourism on islands such as Santorini and Mykonos.

society.q: During the 2022 energy shock, Greece's annual inflation rate peaked at roughly what level?
society.fact: ELSTAT put inflation at 12% in September 2022; the EU-harmonised rate of 12.1% was the highest since Greece joined the euro, with energy prices up over 50% year on year.

society.q: Greece's 2021 census counted roughly how many residents?
society.fact: The final count of 10,482,487 was down about 3% on 2011; births fell, deaths rose, people emigrated, and 12 of the country's 13 regions lost population.

society.q: Since reforms adopted during the debt crisis, what has been the standard retirement age in Greece?
society.fact: Retirement at 67 applies with 15 years of contributions; workers with 40 years of contributions can retire at 62.

society.q: What is the name of Greece's single online portal for public services, launched in 2020?
society.fact: Launched in March 2020 as the pandemic began, it lets citizens get documents such as sworn statements and prescriptions with a few clicks.

society.q: What is the popular name of Greece's scheme offering residence permits to non-EU nationals who buy property?
society.fact: Launched in 2013, it became one of Europe's most popular such schemes, with Chinese buyers the largest group, and has been blamed for pushing up housing costs.

society.q: By roughly how much did Greece's economy shrink in 2020, the first year of the pandemic?
society.fact: The fall of around 9% was among the steepest in the EU because of Greece's heavy reliance on tourism; growth of over 8% followed in 2021.

society.q: In April 2024, Greece raised its gross monthly minimum wage to what amount?
society.fact: It was the fourth rise since 2019, when the minimum wage was €650; the government set a target of €950 by 2027.

society.q: By 2024, Greece's unemployment rate had fallen to roughly what level?
society.fact: The annual average was 10.1% in 2024, down from 11.1% in 2023 and 12.4% in 2022; it dipped to 9.4% in December 2024 but was still the second-highest rate in the EU.

society.q: In August 2022, Greece exited which EU monitoring regime that had followed its bailouts?
society.fact: Enhanced surveillance had been in place since the third bailout ended in 2018; its end was marked by the government as the close of a 12-year chapter.

society.q: In 2022, Greece recorded its lowest number of births in modern records, roughly how many?
society.fact: Deaths that year numbered 140,801, nearly double the 76,541 births; births were down 10.3% on 2021, according to ELSTAT.

society.q: In October 2022, Greece's electricity grid ran for several hours entirely on what, for the first time?
society.fact: Grid operator IPTO reported that wind, solar and hydro met 100% of demand for about five hours on 7 October 2022.

society.q: In 2021, Greece introduced a special visa aimed at attracting which kind of worker to live in the country?
society.fact: The digital nomad visa targets remote workers employed abroad; applicants must show a monthly income of at least €3,500.

society.q: Greece's public debt peaked in 2020 at roughly what share of its GDP?
society.fact: At just over 200% of GDP, it was the highest ratio in the EU; strong growth and inflation brought it down to about 150% by 2024.

society.q: What was the name of the subsidy card Greece introduced in 2023 to help households with grocery bills?
society.fact: It followed the 2022 'Fuel Pass' for motorists; payments were loaded onto a digital card and scaled by household size and income.

society.q: What was the name of Greece's national plan for spending EU post-pandemic recovery funds?
society.fact: Approved in 2021, Greece 2.0 channels over €30 billion in EU grants and loans into green, digital and employment projects.

society.q: In 2024, Greece raised the minimum property investment for a Golden Visa in Athens and popular islands to what?
society.fact: The threshold had been €250,000 for years; the increase, in force from September 2024, was meant to ease pressure on housing for locals.

society.q: From 2025, cruise passengers landing on Santorini and Mykonos in high season pay a fee of how much?
society.fact: The levy applies from June to September; smaller fees apply to other ports and in low season, with the money earmarked for local infrastructure.

society.q: For 2025, Greece froze new short-term rental registrations in three districts of which city?
society.fact: The freeze, later extended to the end of 2026, covered the first three municipal districts, where platforms such as Airbnb were blamed for soaring rents; a daily tax on short lets also rose.

society.q: 'Spiti Mou' (My Home), launched in 2023, is a Greek state programme offering what?
society.fact: It offered cheap loans to buyers aged 25 to 39 with the state covering most of the interest; demand far exceeded the initial budget.

society.q: In 2020, Greece introduced a flat tax rate of what on the foreign income of pensioners who move their tax residence to Greece?
society.fact: The 7% rate applies for 15 years, part of a push to attract retirees and wealthy foreigners after the crisis.

society.q: From 2024, Greece replaced its hotel 'stayover tax' with a levy named after what?
society.fact: The 'climate crisis resilience fee' is charged per night, higher in summer and for five-star hotels, after the wildfires and floods of 2023.

society.q: In April 2025, the Greek gross monthly minimum wage rose to what amount?
society.fact: It was the fifth rise since 2019 and worth about €1,000 a month gross to full-time workers, who in Greece are paid 14 monthly wages a year.

general.q: Which mountain, the highest in Greece, was said to be the home of the gods?
general.fact: Olympus' highest peak, Mytikas, rises to about 2,918 m and was first climbed only in 1913.

general.q: Which sea lies between mainland Greece and Turkey?
general.fact: In myth, the Aegean takes its name from King Aegeus of Athens, who threw himself into the sea believing his son Theseus was dead.

general.q: The word 'alphabet' comes from 'alpha' plus which other Greek letter?
general.fact: Adapted from Phoenician script, the Greek alphabet was the first to use separate letters for vowels.

general.q: Which city hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
general.fact: Spyridon Louis, a Greek water-carrier, won the 1896 marathon and became a national hero.

general.q: In 2004, Greece's men's football team stunned Europe by winning which tournament?
general.fact: Greece beat hosts Portugal 1-0 in the Lisbon final, thanks to a header by Angelos Charisteas.

general.q: Which self-governing peninsula in northern Greece is home to 20 Orthodox monasteries?
general.fact: Women have been barred from Mount Athos for over a thousand years, under a rule known as the avaton.

general.q: The whitewashed villages of Oia and Fira perch on the volcanic caldera of which island?
general.fact: Santorini's huge Bronze Age eruption (c. 1600 BCE) buried the town of Akrotiri, preserving it like a Greek Pompeii.

general.q: Feta cheese is traditionally made mainly from which milk?
general.fact: Since 2002, 'feta' has been an EU Protected Designation of Origin: only brined cheese from designated parts of Greece may use the name.

general.q: How many horizontal stripes are on the flag of Greece?
general.fact: The nine blue and white stripes are popularly said to stand for the syllables of 'Eleftheria i Thanatos' ('Freedom or Death').

general.q: What is the longest river flowing entirely within Greece?
general.fact: About 300 km long, the Aliakmonas runs from the Pindus mountains to the Thermaic Gulf near Thessaloniki.

general.q: What is the largest island in Greece?
general.fact: Crete's Samaria Gorge, about 16 km long, is one of Europe's most popular hikes.

general.q: What prize did winners receive at the ancient Olympic Games?
general.fact: Olympic wreaths were cut from a sacred wild olive tree; laurel wreaths were the prize at the Pythian Games in Delphi instead.

general.q: Which rocky hill in Athens is crowned by the Parthenon?
general.fact: Acropolis means 'high city'; many Greek cities had one, but Athens' is by far the most famous.

general.q: Which Greek dish layers aubergine and spiced minced meat under a thick béchamel topping?
general.fact: Moussaka's béchamel crust was popularised in the 1920s by chef Nikolaos Tselementes, who brought French techniques into Greek cooking.

general.q: What is the last letter of the Greek alphabet?
general.fact: Omega means 'big O' and omicron 'little o'; together, alpha and omega came to mean the beginning and the end.

general.q: Which group of monasteries in Thessaly is perched on top of towering rock pillars?
general.fact: Meteora means 'suspended in the air'; monks once reached some monasteries only by ladders or by nets hauled up with a winch.

general.q: Which traditional Greek wine is flavoured with pine resin?
general.fact: The taste is thought to date back to ancient times, when wine jars were sealed with pine resin to keep the air out.

general.q: What do Greeks call their own country?
general.fact: The country's official name is the Hellenic Republic; the English word 'Greece' comes from the Latin 'Graecia'.

general.q: Which port, linked to Athens since ancient times, is Greece's busiest?
general.fact: Themistocles fortified Piraeus in the 5th century BCE, and the Long Walls once joined it to Athens.

general.q: The White Tower is the best-known landmark of which Greek city's waterfront?
general.fact: Once a notorious Ottoman prison nicknamed the 'Tower of Blood', it was whitewashed in the 1890s and renamed the White Tower.

general.q: Mastic, a resin harvested from shrubs, is produced on the southern part of which Greek island?
general.fact: Southern Chios has around two dozen 'mastic villages'; in Pyrgi, houses are covered in black-and-white geometric patterns called xysta.

general.q: What is the highest mountain on Crete?
general.fact: The Idaean Cave on its slopes is one of two Cretan caves that myth claims as the childhood hideaway of the god Zeus.

general.q: Kalamata olives come from which region of the Peloponnese?
general.fact: These almond-shaped, dark purple olives are named after Kalamata, Messenia's capital and largest city.

general.q: Which mountain, sacred to Apollo and the Muses, rises above the sanctuary of Delphi?
general.fact: Today Mount Parnassus is a national park and also hosts one of Greece's largest ski centres.

general.q: On which island was much of the 2008 film 'Mamma Mia!' shot?
general.fact: Scenes were filmed at the clifftop chapel of Agios Ioannis Kastri, which has since become a popular wedding spot.
